source.title: RULE: Reinforcement UnLEarning Achieves Forget-Retain Pareto Optimality
source.authors: Chenlong Zhang; Zhuo-Ran Jin; Hong-Bang Yuan; Jia-Heng Wei; Tong Zhou; Kang Liu; Jun Zhao; Yubo Chen

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. Figure 5 is described in the text but its plotted values are not given numerically.
record.tranche_reason: The study tests whether post-unlearning fine-tuning restores targeted knowledge and reports that RULE resists this relearning. This challenges broad fine-tuning recovery claims while supporting a qualified counter-method result.
record.gate_note: The reported attack result is in Figure 5: RULE is followed by fine-tuning on the original forget passages. Other unlearning and utility comparisons are not post-unlearning attack tests. The paper mentions extraction attacks in its introduction but those are cited background, not tested results.
record.test_reason: Appendix D.7 fine-tunes the RULE-unlearned llama3-8b-Instruct on the original RWKU forget passages, following the WMDP relearning setup. It reports whether the targeted knowledge comes back. That bears on B (recovery by fine-tuning) and on F (a newer method claiming to resist it). The main tables are unlearning and utility comparisons with no attack, so they do not test A, C, D or E.
record.authors_conclusion: The record over-weights robustness. The authors' main conclusion is that RULE, a refusal-boundary RL method trained on about 12% of the forget set and 8% synthesized boundary data, gives more natural refusals and better forget quality than GA/NPO/SimNPO. They also claim forget–retain Pareto optimality and generalisation to unseen queries. Resistance to relearning (Fig. 5) is a brief appendix claim: RULE keeps high forgetfulness after fine-tuning on the forget passages.
record.recipe_differences: RULE is a refusal-based method with supervised rejection steering followed by reinforcement learning over forget and synthesized boundary queries; it is not one of the original unlearning methods named in the claim. The robustness test applies subsequent fine-tuning on original forget passages.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported robustness result is specific to fine-tuning on original forget passages; other attack types and settings are not evaluated.
record.peer_reviewed: NeurIPS 2025 (venue stated in the record; paper text says preprint, under review)
record.problems: The robustness result is reported only as a plot, without numeric values or uncertainty. The study does not state the amount of fine-tuning data or compare with a model that never learned the target. The robustness experiment tests one model and one relearning attack; it does not establish resistance to other attacks.
record.rows_left_out: No other post-unlearning attack results are reported. The paper's main unlearning tables are not recovery-attack tests.

untested.parts: No attack is applied to the baseline methods (GA, NPO, SimNPO). Unlearning is never shown to reach chance-level knowledge with robustness to simple attacks.

Relearning on unrelated or loosely related data, or on small subsets of the forget set, is not tested. The relearning set size and hyperparameters are not stated. Only one model and one benchmark (RWKU) are used.
No activation ablation or analysis of whether a refusal-based method blocks access rather than deletes knowledge.
Rephrasing, jailbreaks, other languages and in-context attacks are not tested.
Resistance to ablation, quantization, prompting attacks and other relearning data is not tested. Relearning is not tested on MUSE or llama3.1.

missing.what: Plotted Forget and Retain scores over relearning steps 0–200, plus the relearning data amount and hyperparameters. These are needed to judge whether forget scores rise at all.

record.verdict_notes: RULE trains refusal behaviour, scored by regex refusal templates, rather than removing knowledge. Its forget ROUGE (27.7) is well above zero, and retain quality drops from 87.6 to 73.7. A refusal policy resisting relearning does not show deletion, and C-type probing is absent. The paper text says 'Preprint. Under review'; the NeurIPS 2025 venue in the record is not confirmed by the text.

versions.untested_parts: The paper reports unlearning and utility evaluations, but does not test the full version's claim that near-chance targeted knowledge remains unrecoverable by simple attacks, including against a model that never learned the knowledge.
Tests fine-tuning on original forget passages only. The amount of relearning data is not stated; unrelated or loosely related examples and other relearning sets are not tested.
Activation-direction ablation and evidence that unlearning blocks access rather than deleting knowledge are not tested.
Low-bit quantization of unlearned weights is not tested.
Prompt rephrasing, jailbreaks, other languages, and in-context recovery are not tested.
Tests RULE against subsequent fine-tuning on original forget passages only; resistance to ablation, quantization, prompting, and other attacks is not tested.

rows.subject: llama3-8b-Instruct
rows.operation_detail: After RULE unlearning, fine-tune on the original forget passages to test relearning.
rows.measure: Forgetfulness / Forget score after relearning fine-tuning
rows.note: The authors describe RULE as maintaining high forgetfulness after re-exposure and as resisting relearning. Numerical values and the amount of fine-tuning data are not stated.
rows.check: The state is right for B only on the authors' words; no value can be read. The caption says RULE is 'maintaining high forgetfulness even after re-exposure', but the plotted Forget/Retain values, the relearning set size and the learning rate are not given. The body text hedges ('resistance (or susceptibility)'). For F the same result reads as observed, meaning the method resisted. There is no comparison with baselines (GA/NPO) under relearning and no never-trained reference. Baseline and value should stay 'figure only', not be treated as measured.

tranche.reason: T5 covers results showing a version is wrong or partial. Appendix D.7 reports a relearning attack that, by the authors' explicit words, does not restore the forgotten knowledge for RULE. That is a result showing B does not hold for this method. Evidence is weak (figure-only, one model).

source_check.notes: The relearning result is figure-only, from one appendix paragraph: no values, data amount, learning rate or baseline methods under the same attack. RWKU uses ROUGE-L, so 'near chance' does not apply. Text v1 says 'Preprint. Under review.'; the NeurIPS 2025 venue is not in the text.

statements.correction: RULE, llama3-8b-Instruct, RWKU: after unlearning, fine-tuned on the original forget passages (WMDP relearning setup), plotted over 0-200 steps (Fig. 5). The caption says RULE resists relearning and keeps high forgetfulness. No numbers, data amount or baseline methods are given.
statements.problem: Gives no numbers for RULE, only lists it among counter-methods that 'leave forgotten knowledge near chance after relearning'. The text never says near chance for RULE. RWKU is scored with ROUGE-L, so there is no chance level. The attack data, the original forget passages, matches none of the listed relearning data types exactly.
